notes.meaning: Jesus foretells His suffering, death, and resurrection. He explains that the Jewish ruling leaders—the elders, chief priests, and scribes—will reject Him, but this was all part of God's saving plan. The Messiah would not set up an earthly kingdom by force, but would enter His glory through death on the cross.

Jesus tells everyone listening what it costs to follow Him. A disciple must put aside selfish desires and be ready to suffer hardship or even death every single day. Following Jesus is not an easy road of comfort, but a daily choice to live completely for God.

differ.view: Jesus is giving a gospel invitation that outlines the terms of salvation, demanding that sinners surrender self and follow Him with loyal obedience.
Taking up the cross is an everyday duty of practical holiness, meaning that any day lived without carrying a cross is considered wasted.
This call describes the ongoing burden of faithful discipleship rather than the initial requirement for a sinner to be saved.

notes.meaning: Trying to protect one's earthly life and selfish interests leads to losing eternal life with God. Giving up one's life and desires for the sake of Jesus leads to true and lasting salvation. In God's kingdom, a person gains life by surrendering it to Christ.

A person could win all the wealth, power, and honor in the world and still end up ruined. To lose one's soul means losing one's very self at the final judgment. Nothing in the entire universe can make up for the loss of eternal life.

People often worry about what others think and feel ashamed to stand up for Jesus and His teaching. Jesus warns that whoever turns away from Him out of shame will be rejected when He returns in glory. On that final day, the Son of Man will come surrounded by His own majesty and the splendor of the Father and the holy angels.

Jesus promises that some who were standing there would see the kingdom of God before they died. Many commentators understand this as pointing to the transfiguration just days later, where three disciples saw a preview of His divine glory. Others understand it as the resurrection and the powerful spread of the gospel starting at Pentecost.

differ.view: This promise was fulfilled when Jesus received the kingdom at His ascension and began His heavenly reign, as distinct from His final coming in glory.
The prophesied earthly kingdom was postponed because the nation rejected the Messiah, so the transfiguration served as a visual guarantee of that future reign.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern critics argue that Jesus expected His final return to occur within the lifetime of His listeners.

notes.meaning: Jesus climbs a mountain to pray, taking Peter, John, and James with Him as His inner circle. Luke says this happened about eight days later because he counts the starting and ending days, while other Gospels count six intermediate days. Jesus was lifted up into heavenly glory while engaged in prayer, giving His disciples hope after hearing about His death.

While Jesus was praying, His divine glory shone through His human body. His face changed in appearance, and His clothes became dazzling white like flashes of lightning. This holy radiance gave the disciples a brief glimpse of the King of Glory.

Moses and Elijah suddenly appear and begin talking with Jesus on the mountain. Moses represents the law and Elijah represents the prophets, showing that the whole Old Testament points to Jesus. Luke refers to them simply as men, highlighting that Jesus is far greater than either of them.

Moses and Elijah appeared in heavenly glory to talk about the departure Jesus was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. The word for departure refers to an exodus, picturing His death, resurrection, and ascension as God's great rescue of His people from sin. Even in the middle of wonderful brightness, Jesus stayed focused on His coming sacrifice.

Peter and the other two disciples had grown heavy with sleep during the long night of prayer. When they shook off their drowsiness, they saw Jesus shining in glory with the two prophets standing beside Him. God ensured they were awake so they could serve as eyewitnesses of His majesty.

As Moses and Elijah started to leave, Peter eagerly suggested making three shelters to keep all three of them there. He spoke without understanding, wrongly placing Jesus on equal footing with Moses and Elijah. Peter wanted to remain in the glory of the mountain rather than go down to face the cross.

While Peter was still speaking, a cloud came down and wrapped around them. This bright cloud was the visible presence of God, just like the cloud that appeared over Mount Sinai. The disciples felt great fear and awe as the divine glory enveloped them.

God the Father speaks out of the cloud to announce that Jesus is His chosen Son. He commands the disciples to listen to Jesus above all others, fulfilling the promise of a prophet like Moses. Moses and Elijah were honored servants, but Jesus is the ultimate authority to whom everyone must submit.

When the heavenly voice finished speaking, Moses and Elijah were gone, and Jesus was left alone with the disciples. Jesus told them not to share what they had seen until after His resurrection. The disciples obeyed and kept the vision to themselves, realizing the time was not yet right to tell the crowd.

The next morning, Jesus and the three disciples climbed down from the mountain after spending the night there. A great crowd of people was waiting to meet Jesus as soon as He reached the bottom. He returned immediately from the peaceful glory of heaven into the broken struggles of the world.

A man from the crowd cries out desperately and kneels down, begging Jesus to look with pity on his son. He explains that the boy is his only child, which made the tragedy even deeper for the family. In that culture, losing an only child meant the end of the family line and name.

The father explains how an evil spirit attacks his son with sudden screaming and violent convulsions. The demon makes the boy foam at the mouth, constantly bruises him, and hardly ever leaves him alone. This shows the cruel and destructive harm that Satan inflicts when he takes control of a life.

The father had already pleaded with the nine disciples who stayed behind to cast out the spirit, but they could not do it. This failure was baffling because Jesus had already given them power to cast out demons. Their weak faith and lack of prayer left them unable to overcome the stubborn evil spirit.

Jesus grieves over the stubborn lack of faith and the twisted thinking of the generation around Him. He was returning from heavenly splendor to a world full of doubt and arguing, yet His patience and mercy remained steady. He immediately tells the father to bring the boy so He can heal him.
